who: Screen reader users who can see
People using speech input after injury
takeaways: When a control has visible text, its accessible name contains that same text.
Voice users say what they see, like “click Search”. If the hidden name is “Find products”, the command fails.
Best practice: start the name with the visible text, then add context, like “Read more about pricing”.
Icon-only buttons have no visible text, so this rule does not apply to them. They still need a name under 4.1.2.
failures: A “Buy” button named “Add to basket” in code
Visible label “Next” with hidden name “Continue to payment”
Extra hidden words added in front of the visible text
check: For each control with visible text, compare it with the name you annotate.
Say the visible label out loud as a voice command. Would it match?
Check that added context comes after the visible words, not before.

quiz.question: Several cards each show a “Learn more” link. You want each link’s name to be unique. What do you annotate?
quiz.why: It contains the visible text and starts with it, so voice users can say what they see. The others drop the visible words.

spec: Annotate the accessible name for every control whose name differs from its visible text.
Write the visible label as the first words of that name.
Note where visible text is an image of text, so the name includes those words too.
review: What would I say to click this?
Does the coded name match the words on screen?
Why is the name different here?
tradeoff: Writers want short visible labels and full hidden names for context. Keep both by adding context after the visible words, or make the visible label clearer.
system: In the button and link components, document that a hidden name must begin with the visible label.
pitch: Voice users click by saying what they read. If the code disagrees with the screen, the button does not exist for them.
